hood, he held that Canada is more than the sum total of its provinces, that the federal government, rather than being a partner with the provincial governments, is a power above and apart, representing national interests which transcend those of the ten provincial governments combined.
While attaching great importance to his so-called people's package, including the charter of rights, the Prime Minister was unresponsive to the equally important concerns of the provincial premiers in matters which affect not merely their regional interests but the well-being of the nation as a whole. The Prime Minister's attitude is a viewpoint that I cannot accept.
The provincial governments, Mr. Speaker, exercise on behalf of the people of those provinces the powers given to them by our present Constitution. Practically every part of this country today is adversely affected by unresolved jurisdictional disputes involving the ownership and management of natural resources, including offshore mineral rights. When the premier of my province states that he does not believe the natural resources of Nova Scotia should be wrestled from the grasp of Nova Scotians, he is only saying what the people of that province want him to say and, by virtue of the Constitution, have the right to expect him to say on their behalf. This is what he must do. If he did not take that stand he would be false to his duty and negligent in the responsibilities imposed upon him by those who elected him.
As one of the first Canadian provinces to have its own flag, Nova Scotians hold their traditions high. We are a proud people, proud of our heritage and proud of the fact that our forebears came to Nova Scotia from many lands across the sea; from Scotland, Ireland, England, France, Germany, Norway, Switzerland and Sweden, to name but a few. Some of my forebears came from the Rhenish Palatinate and some from Hanover in 1753, before Germany existed. All of these people came for one reason or another, to escape religious persecution, to establish new homes on their own lands where they could sink their roots and seek a new way of life free from harassment and persecution.
As Nova Scotians, we believe that the rights accruing to us before confederation are still ours. In fact, the British North America Act states that whatever the provinces had before confederation, such as mineral rights, they were to retain after confederation. This is spelled out in Section 109 of the BNA Act.
The first seed of ownership was planted in 1605 by the commission given to De Monts, that gallant and adventurous French explorer. It was further strengthened by the Royal Charter of 1621 given to Sir William Alexander. Then there were the treaties of Utrecht and Paris in 1713 and 1763. Our claims were expanded by the commissions of Cornwallis and other governors, as well as by the creation of the legislative assembly in 1758 and legislation passed by the government of Nova Scotia between 1758 and 1867.
From these facts it should be noted that our claims as Nova Scotians to our province and our mineral rights go back over many centuries, and I say to you, sir, that we are not about to
give them up because of a unilateral decision made to gratify the ego of one man. Our claims to offshore mineral rights are now threatened by this government, and I cite this example to indicate that the solution to our problems does not necessarily require constitutional amendments; what is required is a recognition that often the national and regional interests of the country are inseparably related.
The provincial governments must, therefore, be treated as equal partners of the federal government in the policy-making process through which solutions to these problems must be found. However, when the provincial governments made it clear that any amendments to the Constitution should guarantee their rights to the ownership of natural resources and that the priority of provincial economic policy should be reaffirmed and entrenched, the Prime Minister responded that he was not prepared to bargain, in his words, freedom for fish or fundamental rights for oil. Is it any wonder that under these circumstances the first ministers' conference ended in failure.
The proper thing to do at that point, in my opinion, would have been to temporarily set aside all issues other than patria-tion and agreement on an amending formula which even then, in all probability, could have been reached. However, this course of action did not suit the Right Hon. Prime Minister who, instead, decided to embark upon a course of unilateral action to both repatriate and amend the Constitution despite warnings from most of Canada's premiers that such action would have dire consequences for confederation.
Patriation per se is not a matter of disagreement among the Canadian people. Practically all are agreed that our Constitution should be our own statute, passed by our own Parliament and enshrined in this Parliament. 1 agree with that. It is equally true to say that patriation of our Constitution is not a matter of widespread public concern even after this Liberal government spent millions of dollars on television advertising to tell Canadians that life would be uncertain if the British North America Act did not return to Canada.

through you, sir, it is high time it took some action on these urgent economic problems.
Unfortunately, these problems do not seem to concern the Right Hon. Prime Minister. In my view, today he is a man on a mission, on a crusade to change if not the world, then at least Canada, in order to assist in reflecting his ideological and philosophical preferences, with never a thought for the wishes of the Canadian people. This man is on the last lap of his political career. Whether that lap takes one year or another election does not make any difference. He sees what he thinks is best for Canada and, with the single-mindedness of the true believer, is determined against all odds to achieve it. Call it what you like, disguise it as you will, what he seeks for Canada today resembles a socialist dictatorship in my view. If you do not like that term we can call it a centralized paternalistic system, where free choice is limited and where state control is excessive. He proposes that the collective should replace individualism, all in the name of the common good of the average citizen. I say to this House, that the common man's individual liberties will be the casualties.
As the Right Hon. Prime Minister points out in all his writings, his background and leanings do not favour British parliamentary democracy nor a constitutional democracy. He knows better than the average Canadian that if he succeeds in getting human rights and language rights entrenched in the Constitution in the manner he proposes, parliamentary democracy in this country is dead, as will be the monarchy.
Inevitably, Canada will become a republic with a presidential system under the Prime Minister's plan. Make no mistake, the constitutional proposal is entirely that of the Prime Minister, no one else, and he is pushing this proposal with all the force at his command.
What do we see from this side of the House? We see an uncritical group of Liberals blindly following the Pied Piper who blows the flute and leads them over the cliff to their destruction. Occasionally one will surface like Moby Dick and blow his spume into the air, then disappear below the surface, never to be seen again until he somehow reappears in his place to vote as his master dictates.
The over-all effect of this action and this resolution will be that the federal government will intrude ever deeper into our daily lives. There may be some who will claim I am being too critical of the Right Hon. Prime Minister, but I am merely stating truths as he has publicly recorded them. In fact, when Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Pelletier joined the Liberal Party in 1965, after taking a leave of absence from the NDP, they issued a prepared statement which said in part:
The undersigned are still following the same goals-they are continuing to adhere to the same political ideologies that they have for a long time set forth in "Cite Libre." We don't repudiate any of our convictions. We have only resolved to pursue elsewhere and in other ways the intellectual and social struggle which has always claimed us.
When he was justice minister he was taunted with some of his former writings and he responded by saying "everything I wrote I stand by". Three years later-and this is one of the benefits of being in this House for a long time because one can

remember these things-while defending a political decision he said, "I acted on the information I have been accumulating since I was three years old".
This leads me to ask what information, what ideas have formed the basis for the right hon. gentleman's actions. He has pinpointed three main sources for his ideas. In 1971 the Prime Minister said:
In my youth the people who influenced me the most were the Christian existentialists like Mounier. In his last key editorial before his death Emmanuel Mounier wrote in his review "Esprit", "The proletariat must be allowed to continue the positive work of the communist party while eliminating all the poisons which are mixed therein. Such is one of our principal tasks for tomorrow."
In 1966 Mr. Trudeau stated that he found Professor Harold Laski of the London School of Economics "the most stimulating and powerful influence" he had encountered. Laski's single most important book, "A Grammar of Politics", which the Prime Minister studied, laid out these central principles:
The necessarily federal character of society; the incompatibility of the sovereign state with that economic world order so painfully struggling to be born (communism); the antithesis between individual property rights in the essential means of production and the fulfilment of the democratic idea; the thesis that liberty is a concept devoid of real meaning except in the context of equality, there cannot, in a word, be democracy unless there is socialism.
In 1976 Prime Minister Trudeau said:
In terms of economics, you know, I spent two years studying with Schumpeter and two years studying with Leontief, and if you want to know who is formenting my economic thinking you'd do better to think in terms of Leontief and Schumpeter.
I found that Schumpeter was Prime Minister Trudeau's Harvard professor. As his major work the professor wrote "Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy" in which he said:
I have tried to show that a socialist form of society will inevitably emerge from an equally inevitable decomposition of capitalist society.
So it may reasonably be said that the Prime Minister's ideas drawn from the writings of Schumpeter, Laski and Mounier have remained basically the same for the past 30 years.
Let us now look at some of the Prime Minister's writings and compare them with his more recent statements and actions to see how they affect Canadians and will affect Canadians in the immediate future. In 1961 he said:
I should like to see socialists feeling free to espouse whatever political trends or to use whatever constitutional tools happen to fit each particular problem at each particular time.
Is that not exactly what the Prime Minister is doing today, using whatever tools suit him and suit this particular problem? What did Mr. Trudeau say in 1961 before he was Prime Minister.

The people of Canada are facing the most serious constitutional crisis since confederation. As the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) has often stated, the crisis has come about as a result of years of negligence and indifference on the part of the Liberal party.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has adopted an intransigent attitude on the question of constitutional change. All of the provinces have been made to feel they are simply fifth wheels on Ottawa's chariot. The provinces are realistic in demanding consultation in order to determine the shape and style of a new Canada.
Canada's future must be decided by the provinces and the federal government in council together. Let me say this, the future of Canada will not and cannot be decided by one man, Pierre Trudeau-

speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext: Well, Steve, at least you are funny.

I do not intend to be funny. I think this is a very serious and pertinent topic, and I do not consider it to be funny. The minister says I am trying to be amusing. It is Friday afternoon; I think we can inject a little bit of humour, but this is a serious matter and I wish he would take my remarks as a serious speech.
I personally feel that the Constitution should be patriated unchanged, except for an amending formula and that amendments should be made in Canada by agreement with the provinces. I say with some confidence that the provinces would all be ready to settle for less power if they could be assured of more consideration by and consultation with the federal government. Let me say that one more time. I say with some confidence that the provinces would all be ready to settle for less power if they could be assured of more consideration by and consultation with the federal government.
You know they will never agree to that.

You would be surprised.
The requirements on what a workable constitution for a federal state must do for its people are indeed stiff. First of all, any constitution, and particularly a federal one like ours, is the general directing plan for the common life of its people. It is the supervisor of the life of the society. But the people who share in a federal system take different views of life and opportunity. Those views are ingrained in them by history, experience, occupation and inherited attitudes. Our greatest mistake in a federal system is to be unhappy because we cannot live in close unity like a loving family. If we were like that, we would not be struggling to live under a federal system.
1 believe this struggle arises largely out of excessive centralization of power in Ottawa. The malfunctioning of the party system in Canada is one of the results of this excessive centralization.
The policies of the Liberal Party have produced an acute polarization of votes in this country. There was originally- and this is still unresolved-a conflict between the Francophone and Anglophone communities.
[ Translation]
A conflict due to a large extent to the personality of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). And I quote in this regard journalist Jacques Poisson who wrote in the newspaper Le Devoir dated February 9:
Mr. Trudeau is, at one and the same time and to various degrees, the spoilt brat, the constitutional despot . .. the poisoner of the Canadian political climate.

My colleague, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) read something about Canada in the New York Times of February 8. 1 appreciated the hon. member's remarks, but why did he not read the article in Le Devoir of February 9? All told, Mr. Trudeau's public personality embraces, in varying degrees, a tyrannical brat, constitutional despot. . . crazed manipulator of human marionettes, demon of paradox-
I do not even know some of these words.
-expert. . . intimidator, master of contempt, poisoner of Canada's political climate, a narcissist searching for a cosmic mirror in which to reflect his ego.
Constitution, c'est MOl; democracy, c'est MOI; reason, c'est MOI; common sense, c'est MOI.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Who wrote that?

This is a great article by Jacques Poisson in Le Devoir on February 9. I noticed that Pravda has also endorsed the Prime Minister and what he is doing here in Canada. With friends like that, who needs enemies?
Today there is an emerging conflict between east and west. Canada is a land of diversity. Our Constitution must therefore contain enough flexibility in its terms to enable us to come to compromises that will let us flourish in our diversity.
My father brought his family here from Poland and the Ukraine in 1929. Veen priyeekhav do Kanadi: that means "He came to Canada". My father did not come just to one town, he did not come just to one province. He came to Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Hear, hear! Come on over, Steve.

He came to the Canada as seen through the eyes of our Fathers of Confederation which, despite those strained economic times, still offered freedom, opportunity and prosperity.
In this debate on the Constitution what we are really doing is acknowledging the uncomforting reality that the vision and hopes of men like my father and of generations before him may never more prevail in Canada.
The Liberal government has presented a resolution which contains a Canadian charter of rights and freedoms which makes no reference to the affirmation that "the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God" as it is stated in the Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960 brought in by the Progressive Conservative government of that day. The opportunity and prosperity which is sought by all those coming to Canadian shores, in addition to cherished freedom, is also being undermined by this government.
The amendment presented by my colleague, the hon. member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) reiterated a right which had been given to Canadians by the

February 20, 1981
The Constitution
aforementioned bill of rights, and that was "the right of the individual to enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law". This right now is being threatened.
The vision of a country which offered opportunity to pursue goals and aspirations in freedom has for many years attracted peoples from different lands to our country. Canada is people, and it is this very distinctive characteristic of our different peoples within Canada that distinguishes us from our southern neighbour and other anglophone countries in the world.
It is this embracing of the diversities of English-speaking Canada and the distinctiveness of French-speaking Canada that truly reflects the Canadian identity. It is the multicultural character of our country, profound in history and rich in traditions, which must be fostered and protected if we are truly to respect individual and collective freedoms.
I must say that I telephoned the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon-or my office did-to say I would be speaking. I hoped the minister would be in the House. I know he is busy, but as a former minister of multiculturalism I wanted him to hear some of the things I have to say this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext: Your heart is in the right place.

The Liberal government has done nothing to promote a sincere and significant contribution to the development of multiculturalism in Canada. The so-called permanent policy on multiculturalism and its present minister are a shame. Just what is Canada without the recognition of its diverse cultural origins or without the official acknowledgement that over one-third of our population is neither of French nor English origin?
Multiculturalism goes beyond the entertainment novelty of song and dance. It is a history, a language and a way of life contributing to the Canadian social environment. It is certainly not something to be drummed out at election time or when the government needs to improve its public relations image.
The present minister in the Liberal government is a perfect example of what I have just said. That is why I said I telephoned his office. I wanted him to be aware of what I am saying to him today. One wonders about his priorities. Is he really promoting the multicultural nature of this country or is he concentrating on selling the Liberal government?
The former.

He is the minister of propaganda, the Goeb-bels of the Liberal Party.
The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada recognizes the multicultural reality of the Canadian society and is committed to developing this premise. We should not simply accept or tolerate Canada's multicultural nature. We must celebrate it as a formidable guarantee of our uniqueness as a nation and our continued diversity and freedom as a people.
In keeping with this premise, the cabinet of the Leader of the Opposition has reflected this diversity of backgrounds- and I must mention in this context the Hnatyshyns, the Mazankowskis and the Paproskis, that great Irish team! No other cabinet in all of Canada's 112 or 113 years of history has had such a wide representation of talent and expertise. This cabinet was moving toward the enhancement of the multicultural program by proposing an upgrading of the status of this program within the structure of the Department of the Secretary of State.
In keeping with this commitment, the Leader of the Official Opposition last year established a new program within his office and appointed Michel Lamoureux as his special assistant for multiculturalism; he not only speaks French but also Italian, Spanish and other languages, and before I am finished it will include Ukrainian and Polish. Most Canadians, however, are really unaware of a multiculturalism policy in Canada, and those who are aware of such a policy perceive it only in the context of allowing immigrants to maintain their customs and folk traditions.
In one united and independent Canada, Canadians should enjoy effective equality in political and socioeconomic rights, irrespective of their ethnic origin, religion or mother tongue. All ethnocultural communities, from the Anglo-Celtic and French to the smallest ones, contribute to the Canadian cultural mosaic, and their cultural activities should be given moral and material support by the state in proportion to the groups' willingness to survive.
Section 27 in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in this constitutional resolution refers to multicultural heritage. The section reads as follows:
27. This charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
These three lines are an insult to the non-English and non-French citizens of our country. This section is one of interpretation, not one of recognition that over one-third of Canada's population is neither of English nor of French descent.
I do hope that the Prime Minister of Canada and the Minister of State for Multiculturalism will seriously reconsider section 27 of the resolution and will enshrine in the Canadian Constitution the recognition that is due to the members of Canada's ethnocultural communities.
Hon. members opposite may think this is not a serious matter, and I hope the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) is not laughing at what I have had to say today. I have a lot of respect for francophones across this country as well as for anglophones, and I would like to see the same respect accorded to one third of our people who are neither Anglophone nor Francophone. I hope we will keep this in mind and consider it very seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that at this time of the day my remarks will have to be split into two parts, so I will take the opportunity in my opening remarks to comment in a general way on some of
February 20, 1981

the highlights of this debate which has taken place so far. I have deliberately, as I did in the second reading debate, watched each of the speakers, listened carefully to what they have said and tried to put it into perspective.
I think the highlight of this debate, which is equivalent to the third reading of an ordinary bill, took place outside the House when the young hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) who, having been named the spokesman of his party on constitutional matters and having led the debate on behalf of his party in committee with distinction, moderation and sincerity on national television which covered that committee, went before the television cameras this week, along with three other members of his party, and told the people of Canada that he and the others could not vote for this resolution. It was a difficult thing for those four men to do. I respect that type of courage, not only because it was demonstrated by a member of a party which is different from my own but because it represents to me something that is very important.
This demonstrates that in every party there must always be someone who, on a tremendously important issue like this, will put the principles of his country first before party loyalty. I include in these remarks the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) in our party who, after a great deal of struggle and strain within himself and after talking it over with the caucus, announced that he will vote for the resolution, and he gave his reasons publicly. To my knowledge, not one Conservative member denied him that right. Now we see four members of the NDP saying publicly something which was said by the leader of our party on October 2. I will quote the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville from the press release of his statement, a very simple statement, which reads as follows:
Since I feel so strongly that this resolution ignores federalism-ignores the Canadian way-and will further divide the country, I have informed my leader, Mr. Broadbent, and my caucus that I will oppose this resolution when it comes to a vote in the House of Commons.
Surprise, surprise.

I have heard members of the House attack the party for being divided, and I heard a Conservative member, who disagreed very strongly with the NDP, come to their defence yesterday. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville went on to say in his statement:
-my basic opposition rests on the wrongness of the process.
This is the heart and soul of this entire debate. One cannot build a foundation or a house, let alone a constitution of a nation, unless there is purity of thought and purpose. One can build what only looks like a foundation or a house, but it is not a house unless it receives the time, care and attention it deserves.
1 would think Canadians are now somewhat more proud of Parliament than they were two or three weeks ago. They have heard a member of this party declare his sincere convictions which were different from those of the rest of us; he is one among a hundred. Also they have heard four members of the NDP stand up and declare their sincere convictions. They
The Constitution
know they can put more trust in a party which allows independence of mind on fundamental principles than they can when there is solid voting.
Among the 150 Liberals who sit opposite, I am sure there must be some who are concerned that they are destroying, by their stand in this House, the sincere position of Mr. Claude Ryan, the leader of the Liberal party in Quebec. Also they are destroying-and perhaps they want to-the position of the head of the government of Quebec, the Honourable Rene Levesque. These men are Canadians. The latter honestly confessed that he does not like the Anglos, particularly if they live in the city of Montreal or in London, England, but that he does not have anything against the rest of us.
Who says?

In 1961 he stood up in Ottawa as a member of the Lesage government, when he accepted the presidency of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers, and stated that the only way the federal system would be saved was by co-operation.
He was a Liberal then.
Yes, he was a Liberal then.
Today he is a separatist.
He believed that there was good in Canada, if we worked together and co-operated.
What is he today?
If one asks him today why he left the Liberal Party-
It was because he was a separatist.

-he will say publicly and honestly, as he has done many times, that when he became a minister in the Lesage government he had no trouble getting co-operation from the government of the day from 1960 to 1963, but that he was faced with a new type of co-operative federalism in 1963.
During the Diefenbaker period more agreements were signed by the federal government with the provincial governments than at any other time in the history of confederation. These agreements dealt with matters mostly under provincial jurisdiction, but in the interests of developing a stronger Canada agreements were made with the provinces to carry these things forward.
We have heard in this debate that we would never have had a hospitalization plan or a medicare plan under this type of resolution. But in a constitution, in respect of which one thinks of working together, with sovereign rights held by provinces in certain fields and others held by the federal government, but both agreeing in advance that they will never break apart, one

February 20, 1981

could always get agreement if there was a willingness to co-operate.
I was personally able to make agreements with Premier Duplessis. Surely he was a nationalist. My colleague at that time, the minister of labour, Mike Starr, made agreements with Duplessis concerning education, roads, forestry and power. If we could make agreements with strong nationalists in the province of Quebec who were yielding to no one in their awareness of their distinct culture, then why can other governments not do it?
Unfortunately in 1963 we inherited a prime minister who thought co-operative federalism meant calling the provinces in, sitting them down ten across the desk, listening to the civil servants behind them, and telling those provinces what they were to do. Unfortunately, for this late prime minister, he was up against six or seven of the toughest provincial premiers. It was like murderer's row across from him. There was Stanfield, Smallwood, Lesage, Robarts, Duff Roblin, Manning and Bennett. Who would want to take on those ten fellows and try to tell them what they were going to do? Everyone knows that Premier Lesage ran prime minister Pearson off the field of battle in no time. Pearson had to sacrifice his own ministry to bring peace between the federal government and the provinces.
In the last number of years the Canadian way of doing things by consensus has been steadily destroyed. Today we are debating a way of life in Canada. It has been put best by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) when he said that it was really a question of consensus or confrontation. The same comment was made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and other people. The Canadian way and the only way a federal system will work is when everyone is treated as an equal, regardless of which level of government is concerned, until it comes time to pay, and then there is a little bit of argument. This issue of consensus versus confrontation as a technique was used successfully by governments of all political stripes for over 100 years, but within the last ten years they have experienced failure.
May I call it four o'clock?

speechtext:
that Bill C-238, to amend the Criminal Code (invasion of privacy), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I must confess to the House that I am not the original draftsman of this piece of legislation. Nor is it the first time it has been before the House of Commons. This bill was first introduced in an earlier session of Parliament and spoken to on March 3, 1978, by Mr. Eldon Woolliams, Q.C., who everyone knows who has been here for a while, sat in this House from 1957 until 1980, latterly for the constituency of Calgary North.
There are many members of the House who did not know Mr. Woolliams. On the other, there are many who did know him. I think all of us who knew him, regardless of what side of the House we might sit on, felt him to be a truly estimable Member of Parliament, who, by his background and learning, brought a very finely tuned sense of justice and equity to the work in the House of Commons. If one reviews his background it is interesting to note that he was a practising lawyer, and still is, of great distinction in the province of Alberta. But not many of us know that he was a teacher before he became a lawyer. He distinguished himself as a trial lawyer and as a parliamentarian. He maintained his interest in the law. He was our party's critic with regard to justice and legal affairs. He appeared in that role on many occasions with respect to amendments to the criminal law and other things. He was a special delegate and lecturer for Canada to the United Nations seminar on human and civil rights held in Mexico City in 1961. He was a justice delegate for the Canadian Congress on Peace through Law in Belgrade, Yugoslavia in 1971. He carried himself in the House as an avid political partisan, to be sure, but also as an avid partisan of equity and justice, and reviewer of the law to ensure that the law evolved. He did so to ensure that the individual was not forgotten. It was because of his concern at that time that he brought forward this bill. It was a private bill with respect to certain amendments to the Criminal Code respecting the invasion of privacy.
As the House will remember, we have had some spirited debate in this House on the question of wiretapping and on the question of the necessity for the administration of justice to keep up with technological change while others not so interested in the preservation of order in society were doing so. He was very concerned, while these procedures were being carried out, that we become watchdogs of the rights of individuals in terms of the administration of justice. Mr. Woolliams' finely tuned sense of justice caused him concern about some changes in the criminal law which were made in favour of the individual during the minority Parliament of 1972-74 but which were changed in the Parliament that met later in 1974.
February 20, 1981

This bill raises a number of concerns which were important then, and which I suggest to the House are important now. They are important because of what has happened and what is happening to our society. There seems to be a willingness for society to accept the fact that it is now becoming a society of groups rather than a society of individuals. We have large corporations and large unions. We have advocates of law and order, and I happen to be one of them. But in some cases we have advocates of law and order who tend to downplay the importance of groups and talk about the importance of individuals. We talk about groups and people in terms of statistics. We are always talking about the percentage of unemployed, the percentage of disadvantaged, the percentage of senior citizens and the percentage of our population who are veterans. This is a reflection of a society which has turned inward and forgotten that inside those groups, which compete from time to time, there are individuals who count as well.
The history of criminal law has been in the direction of protecting society. It is an important direction but it ought not be the only direction of criminal law. Mr. Woolliams was concerned that the wiretapping legislation and the ability to govern electronic bugging had moved in this direction too far. What he did was propose a bill which would have preserved a number of things and, hopefully, moved the law back a shade from the direction it had taken. This bill is a simple one. First of all, if enacted it would protect the important right of privacy between the solicitor and his client. This would enable the solicitor and client to discuss openly the case with which they are concerned, in the tradition of the common law, without the fear of electronic bugging. As Mr. Woolliams said, one had to consult with one's client in the middle of a field in order to be sure that your conversation was not being electronically bugged.
This bill would also protect the right of privacy of candidates for political office, enabling them to freely discuss matters with their supporters, friends or with others who were involved after the writ was issued. This bill would guard against the admissibility in a court of law of evidence gained through electronic bugging. This bill which I have proposed today, which is really Mr. Woolliams' bill, would limit the use of evidence in a court of law which had been taken illegally. As hon. members in the House know, the Supreme Court of Canada has gone far beyond this basic principle.
The bill would also provide for the ultimate destruction of evidence obtained through the use of electronic devices two years after the completion of the matter for which it was obtained, the trial or the appeal. In this way, the electronically-obtained evidence would not be left lying around to be dredged up and used inappropriately at some other time.
The most important, and perhaps the most controversial aspect of this bill, is that if enacted it would reinstate the 90-day notification clause to ensure that the person against whom the electronic surveillance was being used, if it was not intended to continue, would have the benefit of knowing that. Under the law he would be notified that it had occurred.
Criminal Code
The purport of all these matters was to bring the law back a wee bit to ensure that the law would not be used against an individual in an improper way. I realize that is a very delicate balance; to balance the rights of society against the rights of the individual, but it is something which we must all guard against.
Those things which had occurred in the evolution of the law offended the finely-tuned sense of justice of the then member for Calgary North. But there is another reason why this bill is timely and why I want the government to consider either allowing this bill to go forward or, failing that, allowing it to go to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Privacy has become important in another way. All members of the House know that the government of which I was a member was working on privacy legislation which would have been introduced. They also know that the government in office has brought forward privacy legislation and coupled it with freedom of information legislation in Bill C-43. That bill is now before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. It was such an important piece of legislation that all of us agreed, notwithstanding the fact there were differences, the bill ought to go forward in one day, and in fact second reading debate on that bill took place in one day.
The whole issue of privacy from the point of view of the individual is there, and I think if we are to consider the question of privacy, then all matters of privacy, including the criminal law aspects, ought to be before that committee so we will know how they impact, criminal and civil one upon the other, and we can judge the evolution of the law in terms of the individual.
As I said earlier, we have become a society of groups. We have forgotten to a great degree the importance of individuals and that one of the most fundamentally important rights of a citizen in a free society is that of privacy. That is, privacy of his files, of personal information, privacy of his personal affairs and the important right of privacy from inappropriate snooping by police and authorities, however well intentioned. They are there to protect society but we must ensure that the zealousness of their pursuit does not override the rights of individuals to a free, unfettered and undisturbed life.
The electronic age is upon us and, as technology grows, the potential for that kind of interference grows as well. And I would ask the House, if it cannot see fit to approve the bill, to at least allow the committee now seized with the review of privacy legislation as part of Bill C-43, to also review it as it applies to criminal law. I daresay if the committee does this, they will find relationships and principles that apply in both fields and we will be doing justice to the subject of criminal law in great measure. But more than that, we will have an opportunity to review the operation of a very significant change in the criminal law of Canada, and in that sense this bill can provide the vehicle for that sort of review.
I do not intend to take up any more time of the House with respect to that. One could speak about how that electronic

That delicate balance is something we should have under constant review and this bill provides the opportunity to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Trade)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Trade)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only want to say a few words. It is ironic to think that in this House we always learn at the last moment that the subjects which most interest us are going to be discussed. I had the opportunity to work with the member who originally moved this motion, Mr. Eldon Woolliams, with whom I also had the opportunity, in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, to discuss the admissibility in a court of law of evidence directly or indirectly obtained through illegal bugging.
Following this long debate in committee, we had introduced through the minister an amendment to Section 178.16 to make it again possible for the judge to refuse this evidence when it might tarnish the image of justice. I am, of course, aware of the debate to which the hon. member referred and which is now going on, especially in the United States, concerning the merit of the American rule of total exclusion. I do not want to give my own opinion on this issue at the present time as I know that other members want to take part in this debate, but even in the United States there is no unanimity among the judges or the members of the legal profession, who opt for one side of the argument or the other according to their approach to all the problems caused by the total exclusion rule, since there is no irrefutable evidence in the United States that this rule has prevented the police from acting within the limits normally allowed by law, as the sponsor emphasized earlier. The data on this issue is still very incomplete and it still remains to be shown that the exemplary nature of the total exclusion rule has had the expected results and that the law enforcement bodies have reacted in the way that the hon. member hopes that our own police forces would react to total exclusion.
On the other hand, the virtually total admissibility rule of English common law has caused other types of problems, since it encourages in fact certain action on the part of those who present this evidence without giving to the judge the possibility of maintaining the normal dignity of our courts. Such a
provision as Section 178.16(2), which has not yet been seriously tested by the courts, would tarnish the image of justice. I hope that it will be tested eventually and that, for once, our courts will show some legal initiative in this regard, and what I anticipate and wish is that this issue will finally be tested against Scottish common law, which does not follow the rule of total exclusion, but still stands out against the virtually total admissibility rule of English common law, by providing a series of criteria which the judge presiding at the hearing can use to exclude evidence according to the seriousness of the offence and the seriousness of the penalty which could be imposed on the accused if found guilty. So, Mr. Speaker, I was hoping that at last this provision would be applied, that at last it would be tested before Canadian courts, and as a result of the discussions we had in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs I was hoping that Canadian courts would imitate or try to imitate the jurisprudential trend which prevails in Scottish common law.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, I took the floor unprepared. I have a lot of documentation on this subject which fascinates me. I would have liked to be able to speak longer in the House but I am only trying to clarify a few points and to explain my own position on the subject. In this respect I would urge our Canadian courts to be more active and I also hope that lawyers and attorneys general will take the issue of Subsection 178.16(2) before the courts so they will be able to rule on it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). In most cases I find myself either agreeing or partially agreeing with what he says on various subjects from day to day as we seem to be on the same wave length. Today I can say that I do not agree with anything he has said on this particular bill. It does not seem that we are talking about the same thing.
This bill does not really talk about the rights of individuals; it gives lawyers and candidates for federal office more rights than the average individual and more rights when they are actually breaking the law. We are not talking about solicitor-client relationships but about lawyers using the telephones, or lawyers' partners or members of their households using telephones in order to break the law.
Talk about the right of the individual sounds very well in this House of Commons. I do not think the right of the lawyer was mentioned once by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton. In Sault Ste. Marie several years ago a lawyer was actively engaged in a conspiracy to traffic in narcotics and the police were having difficulty finding the telephone he used. It turned out to be the barrister's telephone in the courthouse. That makes sense; if you are going to do something illegal, then use the telephone the police are least likely to tap. The police finally got an order to wiretap the barrister's telephone in the
February 20, 1981

courthouse and the evidence was used in a public trial to convict him.
There was a great deal of discussion amongst members of the bar in Sault Ste. Marie at that time about whether this was done in the spirit of the law. I think we came to the conclusion that as lawyers we were officers of the courts and should not be above the law; that at the very least we should be furthering the law and that to have more rights when breaking the law would be unacceptable. But that is exactly what would be proposed by the hon. member opposite, and it surprises me, Mr. Speaker.
We are looking for a delicate balance between the right of the individual and the right of the community as a whole to be protected. In this search for balance, which has been debated many times in this House of Commons, I do not think lawyers and Members of Parliament should have any more rights than the man in the street they are either protecting or representing. In effect, the bill would prohibit the wiretapping of any phone commonly used by a lawyer, and any communication of a candidate seeking election to the House of Commons during the currency of an election campaign. Why stop there? Why not extend this to municipal politicians or provincial politicians who break the law? After we have protected all these people while they break the law using the telephone by assuring that they cannot be wiretapped, then let us extend this to priests, ministers, psychiatrists and anyone who has a confidential relationship with another. While they are breaking the law, let us give them that protection.
It must be kept in mind that a wiretap authorization may be granted only if a judge-it has to be a judge to whom the application is made-is satisfied that it would be in the best interests of the administration of justice to grant the authorization, that other investigative procedures have been tried and have failed-these are all criteria-that other investigation procedures are unlikely to succeed or that the urgency of the matter is such it would be impractical to carry out the investigation of the offence using other investigative procedures only. These are all criteria the judge to whom the application is made can apply. The application is not made to a policeman or a desk sergeant or a duty officer, but to a judge, and it is he who must be satisfied that the criteria are met.
I suggest to the hon. member opposite that the principle that no person is above the law is firmly entrenched in the concept of the rule of law and not men.
There is a very serious case to which 1 should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, and probably most hon. members who have been round the House or involved with Quebec are familiar with it. The case was Roncarelli v. Duplessis. Mr. Duplessis was the premier and attorney general of the province of Quebec. Mr. Roncarelli sued Premier Duplessis, the right honourable, personally for damages arising out of the cancellation of his licence issued by the Quebec Liquor Commission. Mr. Roncarelli was not a professional bailsman-he owned a restaurant-but he provided bail for Jehovah Witnesses who were distributing pamplets in contravention of a Montreal bylaw of
Criminal Code
the day. This bylaw was ultimately struck off the books. At the trial Mr. Roncarelli won his case. He lost at the court of appeal. Finally, at the Supreme Court of Canada, he was successful.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Who was his counsel?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I don't know.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: It was Frank Scott.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has alluded to a very well-known and famous civil libertarian who acted as counsel for Mr. Roncarelli. I think that only adds to the importance of the case because Mr. Scott's ventures into the courts were few and far between, and they were always on very important issues.
This was a landmark decision because it held, in effect, that no man, not even the premier of a province and an attorney general at that, is above the law or can act arbitrarily in disregard of the law.
The hon. member opposite is dealing with lawyers and then political candidates. In the Roncarelli v. Duplessis case the decision of the Supreme Court would suggest that this should not be so but that such persons should be subject to just as much scrutiny, be they the attorney general, a lawyer or a political candidate, if involved in criminal activity, as any ordinary citizen. That is the whole point, Mr. Speaker.
We go further than this, however. In 1977 this Parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment Act which amended section 178.13(1.1) of the Criminal Code to read:
No authorization may be given to intercept a private communication at the office or residence of a solicitor, or at any other place ordinarily used by a solicitor and by other solicitors for the purpose of consultation with clients, unless the judge to whom the application is made is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the solicitor, any other solicitor practising with him, any person employed by him or any other such solicitor or a member of the solicitor's household has been or is about to become a party to an offence.
It is not a case of the client having committed a crime but of the persons indicated above being or about to become, a party to an offence. Parliament thereby recognized that the communications of a solicitor or, more properly stated, a client seeking legal advice from a solicitor, has a unique status in common law jurisdictions.
There is protection in the Criminal Code and there is protection-and I will get to this-given to clients but not to their solicitors who are committing crimes.
However, Parliament also decided that this privilege was not absolute and that where the solicitor or another solicitor practising with him or one of their employees or members of their households has been or is about to become a party to an offence as defined by Section 178.1, of the Criminal Code- they are not simple offences, in fact, they are very serious, including murder, treason, robbery, kidnapping, importing or

February 20, 1981
Criminal Code
exporting narcotics, etc.-a judge could authorize the interception of a private communication by electronic surveillance.
As a safeguard. Section 178.13 (1.2) was enacted which reads:
Where an authorization is given in relation to the interception of private communications at a place described in Subsection (1.1). the judge by whom the authorization is given shall include therein such terms and conditions as he considers advisable to protect privileged communications between solicitors and clients.
In other words, it is not a holus-bolus right to wiretap. The judge can make it mandatory and set out specific terms and conditions which must be adhered to by the police. For instance, monitoring might not be automatic, which is often the case. The tap is put on and the tape is let go for 24 hours before being checked. It could be directed to specific targets. It could be directed to specific individuals with whom the solicitor is dealing, and so on. There is no definitive description given in the section. It is a right, it is a mandatory obligation, and the judge must adhere to it in his examination of the request. The scope is minimized. Further, it is not the normal run-of-the-mill holus-bolus affidavit which usually emanates from the police in situations like this. The affidavit required in these specific circumstances must be quite clear, much more definitive and much more directed to the specific individual and the specific circumstances.
Section 178.12 formerly required that an affidavit filed in support of the authorization set out the names and addresses, if known, of all persons, the interception of whose private communications there are reasonable grounds to believe may assist the investigation of the offence and, if not known, a general description of the place at which the communications are proposed to be intercepted or, if a general description of that place cannot be given, a general description of the manner of interception proposed to be used.
The difficulty with that former provision was that the information required was disjunctive, not cumulative and did not give the judge enough background information.
Recognizing that more information was required for the judge before he could be satisfied that what he was doing was proper and just in the circumstances. Section 178.12 was amended to acquire further information.
I see the logic of my argument is driving the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton out of the House.
Section 178.12 is further amended to require that the names, addresses and occupations, if known, of all persons, the interceptions of whose private communications there are reasonable and probable grounds to believe may assist in the investigation of the offence, a general description of the nature and location of the place, if known, at which the private communications are proposed to be intercepted and a general description of the manner of interception proposed to be used. As well, the affidavit requires the number of instances, if any, on which an application has been previously made in relation to an offence of a person named in the affidavit and on which the application was drawn or no authorization was given, and so forth.
It is a very broad requirement. It is not like walking into your friendly candy store and obtaining permission to wiretap. It is carefully gone over. Affidavits are required and there are safeguards. Once these safeguards are adhered to and a decision is made by a judge, the lawyer who is engaging in criminal activity, the MP or intended MP who is engaged in criminal activity has no further right than any other individual has in Canada.
If you are talking about confidentiality of clients, these safeguards are in the Criminal Code already. The solicitor-client relationship and solicitor-client conversations are protected under the Criminal Code, and rightly so. We are not talking about clients who may be charged with a crime, we are talking about the lawyer who is engaged in a crime. There should be that freedom between clients and their lawyers.
As my allotted time is drawing to a close, I would say that in my opinion the private members' bill, and I say this respectfully, has absolutely no merit and should not be supported. Its dangerous consequences would be to put lawyers and their close associates above the law. If anything, lawyers should be in the vanguard promoting respect for and compliance with law. The hon. member opposite referred to his background. I am a lawyer. I have been a defence counsel, president of a law association and I have been a commissioner of police for a short time. I think I am looking at this problem with some sort of balance.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Have you ever had to go to a lawyer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
I could never afford a lawyer, that is why 1 had to become one.
As well as this extra right given to lawyers, the hon. member is saying it should also go to Members of Parliament. I think this is wrong. Necessary safeguards are in the Criminal Code. The wiretap is the last resort. It requires the authorization of a judge who must be satisfied that the wiretap is necessary and the conditions for it are met. Surely lawyers and potential parliamentarians should be subject to criminal investigation by wiretapping if they are involved in serious crimes. Surely they should have no more rights than the average individual on the street.
1 would implore hon. members not to support this bill. If hon. members want to look at wiretapping in general, and if there is a desire for more protection and more safeguards, that is one thing, but if hon. members say the safeguards are sufficient but, let us just give lawyers more, I say that is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention this afternoon concerns Bill C-238 introduced by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), for whom 1 have the utmost respect. It was typical of the hon. member to mention that the bill was formed and prepared under the direction of a previous member of this House. Before coming to this House I knew about the professional reputation of the hon. gentleman. I am well aware of the standards he upholds in this House and before the Bar of Ontario. I, for one, as a
February 20, 1981

member of the other side of the House have always appreciated his quiet effective manner. He is always a gentleman and he always presents his arguments to this House in a like manner. It is therefore with some regret that I find 1 cannot support this Bill C-238.
Bill C-238 is an act to amend the Criminal Code, the invasion of privacy provisions, to safeguard lawyers and candidates of this House previous to an election. The bill upsets what the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton said. It upsets the delicate balance between the invasion of privacy of the individual and the protection of society against crime. It upsets the right of individuals and the responsibilities of our society to protect its members and citizens.
Bill C-238 would prohibit wiretapping of a telephone, commonly used by a lawyer or a candidate seeking election to the House of Commons during the campaign period. This bill would make lawyers and members of the House of Commons a special class of citizens. I spent 30 years in the practice of law and have just completed one year as the Member of Parliament for Niagara Falls. For neither of those designations would 1 claim a special privilege not granted to ministers, priests or any other member of society who deals with individuals in a very special way, including those concerned with crime.
I appreciate the underlying consideration, that this bill gives protection to the clients of lawyers and constituents of Members of Parliament. I suggest this special status is not required by lawyers or for those they represent. Wiretap orders are not given out lightly by our judiciary. In each and every case the judge balances the rights of the individual against the rights of society, to which I referred a moment ago.
Will we put certain people in our society above the law? We believe in the principle that no person is above the law. That principle ought not to be lightly turned aside. That point was made by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Irwin). To suggest that a political candidate for this House, even if he may be involved in a crime, should have a special privilege denied to others, I cannot accept.
Before a wiretap order is given for a lawyer's telephone, the judge must be persuaded by affidavit evidence that the lawyer is or is about to become a party to an offence. That is a very special and significant provision. The order is not otherwise available to the police.
Except for special cases, a lawyer's telephone cannot be tapped. There is a built-in protection which, in my opinion, is sufficient for the lawyer and client relationship and to protect that principle which we all accept. In my opinion, the same necessity does not arise for a member of this House.
Should the principle in Bill C-238 be extended to make crime a safer business for anyone, even for lawyers? That should not be the case. When a judge grants a wiretap order where a lawyer is involved, the Criminal Code requires that in order to safeguard privileged communications between a lawyer and a client, in accordance with the normal relationship of solicitor and client, other conditions can be inserted by the
Criminal Code
judge if he deems them advisable. In most cases there would be special provisions.
If the premises of this bill are sound, why are MLAs and members of municipal councils not given the same protection?
I have been unable to make a distinction. I accept that the bill was introduced by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton in good faith and with great sincerity. I regret, as I said before, that I cannot accept the bill as having any merit. I do so with great respect for the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, of whom I spoke very highly only a few moments ago.
The bill would be totally unacceptable in the constituency of Niagara Falls. There is no way I can go home tonight, and I hope to be able to after spending two weeks in this wonderful city, the home of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, and have this bill accepted by the residents of Niagara Falls. It just would not be accepted. The people I represent do not wish to put lawyers or candidates for the House of Commons in a special class. We do not want, need or ask for this special privilege and this House ought not to grant it.
Lawyers have a special responsibility to society. 1 firmly believe that. In my early youth at Dalhousie law school in Halifax, Nova Scotia, which I had the honour to attend, we spent a lot of time discussing this fact. Lawyers, not just in Canada but all over the world, have a special responsibility and special duty to society. As the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie said, we are officials of the court. We have special responsibilities. I suggest we need no special privileges.
As lawyers we know that society is a thin veneer. We know that society is a delicate fabric. We know this from our study of the law and of what has happened to societies when the law has not been given the care and attention it has deserved. The place of law in modern society is well known to lawyers. We have a duty to uphold it. Every citizen has a duty to uphold the law, but 1 think most lawyers throughout the world would accept the principle that lawyers have a special duty to uphold the law. They ought not to seek any exemption from it.
If lawyers or candidates for election to this honourable House are involved in crimes and they fall into the net of the wiretap, I say, so be it. It will happen obviously, from time to time; no profession is completely free from the criminal element. I would be wrong to suggest that the profession of law, of which I, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton and the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie are members, is free from the criminal element, but we strive for that freedom. From the very day we enter law school that is drummed into us. It is drummed into us long before we learn about the rule of Rylands and Fletcher that lawyers have a special duty. Never in my years in law at Dalhousie-and I am sure this is true of the honourable institution attended by the two previous speakers-was there any suggestion that as lawyers we should be given any special privileges or any special exemptions from the law of the land or from the rule of law. I think we ought not to ask for that.

February 20, 1981
Criminal Code
As lawyers, like many others in our society today, we are concerned about organized crime in this country. It is a genuine concern. We are concerned that genuine police work is being hampered. I say genuine because lawyers also have a duty to ensure that the police do their duty within the law. When they do not do so, they must answer to the law.
We are concerned that organized crime is finding ways to get around the good laws of this country which are laid down to protect our society. Organized crime is finding ways to enter legitimate business and legitimate industry. This is of grave concern to lawyers, to politicians and to businessmen. There are many in our society who are concerned about this trend in our country and concerned that our neighbour to the south is experiencing a difficulty at this time. If history goes on the way it usually does, when there is a problem in our great neighbour to the south, that problem at a later time is usually found in Canada. This is a great concern to us.
1 ask this honourable House not to support Bill C-238.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since four o'clock we have been listening to lawyers stating both sides of the case. Perhaps a non-lawyer might try to give the verdict.
I may say that whenever any measure having to do with wiretapping comes into this House, we are interested because our basic disposition is to be against it. However, since the time is limited, I had better get to what 1 have to say.
I say quite frankly to my friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that I think those on the other side have made a pretty good case against the proposition in this bill that special consideration should be given to lawyers and candidates in a federal election, but I point out to those on the opposite side that there are five clauses in the bill. They have spent all their time on the one they could easily knock down. I wish they had given some time to clause 1, which has something to do with making it impossible to get an order for continuing authorization at the same time as one gets the original authorization.
I wish they had had something to say about Clause 2, which tries to strengthen the law so that wiretap evidence can be introduced in court only if it has been obtained legally. I think that is a pretty important matter to consider.
Then there is another clause which would reinstate the application of that part of the law, that used to be there, which makes it necessary for persons who have been subject to wiretapping to be notified within 90 days thereafter. Then
there is an interesting clause which suggests that certain materials which have been obtained by a wiretapping should be destroyed after a certain length of time. 1 am not surprised that my friends opposite did not attack these other points because they seem to have some merit.
One thing the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Irwin) said was well put. He said, "If you want to have a look at the whole question of wiretapping, fine; just don't concentrate on the business of a special privilege for lawyers and candidates." I agree with him with respect to the latter, but I think the other matters having to do with wiretapping are such that it would not hurt to have the whole question reviewed by the appropriate committee.
There is still time if hon. members opposite would like to bring forward a motion that the bill not be read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for study.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last participant in this debate, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), has brought his usual wisdom to the subject, for which we thank him. He gave us a number of insights which I believe should be pursued. He did the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and all of us a favour by pointing out what is the main weakness in this particular bill.
1 believe there is nobody in this House who feels very happy about the subject of wiretapping. It is an unpalatable subject in some respects or, to put it more correctly, it has some unpalatable connotations. Anything that can be done to make conditions for permission for wiretapping more stringent is a step in the right direction. The people on this side who have spoken before me have very rightly devoted their time to what would be, if this bill were accepted by this House, a monumental error on our part.
